<type>file</type>
<content>
1: # Testing
2: 
3: celld makes three important promises:
4: 
5: - An acknowledged write is durable.
6: - A cell has one writer at a time. It never has two.
7: - Code written for Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects operates the
8:   same on celld.
9: 
10: We try to break each promise at the layer where a failure shows most
11: clearly. We test the API contract with differential execution against the
12: Cloudflare runtime. We check the coordination protocol against an
13: exhaustively model-checked specification, and we test it with
14: deterministic simulation. We test the full system with fault injection
15: on live fleets.
16: 
17: ## Conformance: two runtimes, one output
18: 
19: We test the compatibility promise differentially. We run each Workers and
20: Durable Objects program twice: once on workerd, the runtime binary that
21: Cloudflare operates in production, and once on celld, on identical bytes.
22: The two outputs must be equal. This shows two facts at once: the program
23: is real Cloudflare code, because workerd accepts it, and celld obeys the
24: contract, because the outputs are equal. A test cannot agree with our own
25: runtime by accident.
26: 
27: The corpus only grows. When celld gets a new API surface, we add fixtures
28: for that surface, and the fixtures must give equal output on the two
29: engines. We also port test suites from workerd itself: the Durable
30: Objects contract, the web-platform globals, and the upstream Web Platform
31: Tests. Before a release, we also replay scenarios through the full
32: `celld` binary in each deployment mode: storage, SQL, alarms, streams,
33: WebSockets, and lifecycle.
34: 
35: ## Specification: exhaustive at small size
36: 
37: The coordination protocol is also specified in TLA+. Heyang Zhou wrote
38: the specifications against celld v0.1.0, and his model checking found
39: four bugs and a split-brain that lost an acknowledged write. All are
40: fixed. None had surfaced in our own review or testing.
41: 
42: Where simulation samples schedules, the checker enumerates them: at a
43: small configuration it visits every reachable state. The model grants
44: the implementation a linearizable object store and perfect shared
45: clocks, so a violation it finds needs no clock skew and no storage
46: anomaly to occur. The invariants are the first two promises at the top
47: of this page: one writer for each epoch, and no acknowledged write
48: lost. The fencing argument itself — that a stale owner's late writes
49: cannot cost an acknowledged write, because the epoch in the key keeps
50: its lineage apart — is checked, not asserted.
51: 
52: Every configuration carries a pinned expected verdict, and most of the
53: verdicts are failures: each failing configuration models a bug the
54: protocol once had, or a deliberately broken checker, and the model
55: must produce the counterexample. A configuration that stops failing
56: has lost its tooth. One tooth had already fallen out when the
57: specifications arrived; we repaired it.
58: 
59: Some specifications model a proposed protocol before it is built. When
60: the fence on write acknowledgments was redesigned, the design-stage
61: check produced an eight-state counterexample against the version it
62: replaced: a dormant cell resumes at its old epoch while its release is
63: in flight, acknowledges a write, and the takeover that follows
64: restores without it. The fix shipped; the counterexample stays as a
65: pinned failure.
66: 
67: The checker has also removed code: celld once sealed a cell's durable
68: history at restore, and the verdicts showed the seal defended only the
69: return of a write that was never acknowledged — an outcome celld does
70: not promise to prevent — while its permanent cut could turn a
71: recoverable ordering slip into a permanent loss. The seal is gone.
72: 
73: The specifications are a hand-synced snapshot, deliberately not in
74: continuous integration: a silently stale gate is worse than none. In
75: practice their updates have landed in the same changes that moved the
76: protocol, and a delta ledger records what the model does not yet
77: describe, including places where the model is weaker than the code
78: rather than wrong. Simulation remains the per-commit ratchet; the
79: model is its exhaustive small-configuration complement.
80: 
81: ## Simulation: the protocol under adversarial schedules
82: 
83: The dangerous bugs live in the coordination: a crash during an ownership
84: handoff, a lease renewal that races a takeover, an alarm that fires
85: against a partially restored cell. These windows are nanoseconds wide and
86: open rarely, so a test cannot wait for them.
87: 
88: Thus the coordination protocol is a
89: [pure decision core](https://github.com/denoland/celld/tree/main/crates/logic)
90: with no I/O of its own: the clock, the randomness, and the object store
91: are interfaces, and a simulator drives the core. The simulated store
92: injects latency, compare-and-swap races, and lost responses; the clocks
93: drift apart; a node can crash at each await point. Scripted adversaries
94: play the cells: a handler that never returns, a write stream that stops
95: halfway. V8 stays out of the simulation, because V8 is not deterministic.
96: 
97: A seeded scheduler drives each run, so a failure is not a fluke: the seed
98: replays it exactly, every time, and we keep the seed until the bug is
99: dead. We examine each property for safety (two writers in one epoch, a
100: lost acknowledged write, an expired lease that comes back) and for
101: liveness (each armed alarm fires, and ownership settles on one node after
102: a crash). A property must survive tens of thousands of seeds, and the
103: core protocols have run through millions of different schedules.
104: 
105: Simulation has a known failure mode: the checker that cannot fail. So
106: we also test the checkers: we run deliberately broken variants of the
107: protocol against the properties, and the properties must find the damage.
108: A suite that stays green against a broken protocol is a broken suite.
109: 
110: ## Live fleets: what simulation cannot see

# Testing

celld makes three important promises:

- An acknowledged write is durable.
- A cell has one writer at a time. It never has two.
- Code written for Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects operates the
  same on celld.

We try to break each promise at the layer where a failure shows most
clearly. We test the API contract with differential execution against the
Cloudflare runtime. We check the coordination protocol against an
exhaustively model-checked specification, and we test it with
deterministic simulation. We test the full system with fault injection
on live fleets.

## Conformance: two runtimes, one output

We test the compatibility promise differentially. We run each Workers and
Durable Objects program twice: once on workerd, the runtime binary that
Cloudflare operates in production, and once on celld, on identical bytes.
The two outputs must be equal. This shows two facts at once: the program
is real Cloudflare code, because workerd accepts it, and celld obeys the
contract, because the outputs are equal. A test cannot agree with our own
runtime by accident.

The corpus only grows. When celld gets a new API surface, we add fixtures
for that surface, and the fixtures must give equal output on the two
engines. We also port test suites from workerd itself: the Durable
Objects contract, the web-platform globals, and the upstream Web Platform
Tests. Before a release, we also replay scenarios through the full
`celld` binary in each deployment mode: storage, SQL, alarms, streams,
WebSockets, and lifecycle.

## Specification: exhaustive at small size

The coordination protocol is also specified in TLA+. Heyang Zhou wrote
the specifications against celld v0.1.0, and his model checking found
four bugs and a split-brain that lost an acknowledged write. All are
fixed. None had surfaced in our own review or testing.

Where simulation samples schedules, the checker enumerates them: at a
small configuration it visits every reachable state. The model grants
the implementation a linearizable object store and perfect shared
clocks, so a violation it finds needs no clock skew and no storage
anomaly to occur. The invariants are the first two promises at the top
of this page: one writer for each epoch, and no acknowledged write
lost. The fencing argument itself — that a stale owner's late writes
cannot cost an acknowledged write, because the epoch in the key keeps
its lineage apart — is checked, not asserted.

Every configuration carries a pinned expected verdict, and most of the
verdicts are failures: each failing configuration models a bug the
protocol once had, or a deliberately broken checker, and the model
must produce the counterexample. A configuration that stops failing
has lost its tooth. One tooth had already fallen out when the
specifications arrived; we repaired it.

Some specifications model a proposed protocol before it is built. When
the fence on write acknowledgments was redesigned, the design-stage
check produced an eight-state counterexample against the version it
replaced: a dormant cell resumes at its old epoch while its release is
in flight, acknowledges a write, and the takeover that follows
restores without it. The fix shipped; the counterexample stays as a
pinned failure.

The checker has also removed code: celld once sealed a cell's durable
history at restore, and the verdicts showed the seal defended only the
return of a write that was never acknowledged — an outcome celld does
not promise to prevent — while its permanent cut could turn a
recoverable ordering slip into a permanent loss. The seal is gone.

The specifications are a hand-synced snapshot, deliberately not in
continuous integration: a silently stale gate is worse than none. In
practice their updates have landed in the same changes that moved the
protocol, and a delta ledger records what the model does not yet
describe, including places where the model is weaker than the code
rather than wrong. Simulation remains the per-commit ratchet; the
model is its exhaustive small-configuration complement.

## Simulation: the protocol under adversarial schedules

The dangerous bugs live in the coordination: a crash during an ownership
handoff, a lease renewal that races a takeover, an alarm that fires
against a partially restored cell. These windows are nanoseconds wide and
open rarely, so a test cannot wait for them.

Thus the coordination protocol is a
[pure decision core](https://github.com/denoland/celld/tree/main/crates/logic)
with no I/O of its own: the clock, the randomness, and the object store
are interfaces, and a simulator drives the core. The simulated store
injects latency, compare-and-swap races, and lost responses; the clocks
drift apart; a node can crash at each await point. Scripted adversaries
play the cells: a handler that never returns, a write stream that stops
halfway. V8 stays out of the simulation, because V8 is not deterministic.

A seeded scheduler drives each run, so a failure is not a fluke: the seed
replays it exactly, every time, and we keep the seed until the bug is
dead. We examine each property for safety (two writers in one epoch, a
lost acknowledged write, an expired lease that comes back) and for
liveness (each armed alarm fires, and ownership settles on one node after
a crash). A property must survive tens of thousands of seeds, and the
core protocols have run through millions of different schedules.

Simulation has a known failure mode: the checker that cannot fail. So
we also test the checkers: we run deliberately broken variants of the
protocol against the properties, and the properties must find the damage.
A suite that stays green against a broken protocol is a broken suite.

## Live fleets: what simulation cannot see

Simulation cannot see the real S3 tail latency, the real kernel and
filesystem behavior, or V8 under memory pressure. The third layer is
therefore a permanent fleet lab: standard VMs from standard providers,
and a real bucket. The workloads rotate: chat rooms under many WebSocket
connections, working sets that shift across tens of thousands of cells
(each cell has a unique checksum), deployment cutovers under load, and
runs that fill the nodes to the memory limit. The lab qualifies each
release, and between releases it pushes the density and the fault
coverage further. Each run makes an archived evidence bundle: the
configuration, the verification sweeps, the node journals, the kernel
logs, and the phase timings. We keep a red run with the same care as a
green run, because a failure that the harness caught is a result, not a
retry.

We inject the faults between verification passes. A pass fetches each
cell through different nodes and compares the durable state exactly: the
status, the body, and the full message ledger. Each run therefore has a
clean picture before the fault and after it. A cell can be unavailable
for a short time while its ownership moves, but its committed state must
stay complete, and a live node must serve that state again.

The scenarios attack every seam that we know:

- Stop a node with `SIGKILL` in the middle of a write stream and delete
  its local database, so recovery can only come from the bucket. Every
  acknowledged write comes back, because the output gate held each
  response until the write was durable.
- Freeze an owner node, write to its cells through other nodes, and
  unfreeze it. The node sees that its lease moved and refuses to serve
  the old state, and each write from the other nodes lands exactly one
  time: one epoch has at most one writer.
- Cut a node off from the bucket. It fences itself, because a node that
  cannot replicate must not own cells.
- Throttle the bucket, so it answers each request with a 429. The engine
  slows to the write rate of the store and does not amplify the
  throttle, because a node that knows its replicated position does not
  ask a slow store for extra listings.
- Stop a full host at the provider level in the middle of a workload.
  Its cells move to the other nodes, and the returning host joins again
  with no duplicate residency.

Across every run of every scenario, no acknowledged write was lost and
no committed state was damaged; the verification sweeps show zero body
faults, zero status faults, and zero lost messages.

## A few numbers we trust

Each number includes the condition of its measurement. A number without
its conditions has no value.

- **The epoch fence holds under contention.** Five hundred claimants
  tried at the same time to own the same cells: 5,500 attempts, one
  writer for each epoch, zero violations.
- **A warm resident request is local.** A request to a resident cell does
  zero bucket operations and returns in p50 ~1.1 ms and p99 ~7 ms (a
  fixed-host measurement). Only a cold activation touches object storage.
- **A durable write waits for a durability proof.** A single node proves
  each write through the bucket, so one storage round trip is the minimum
  latency for that write. A fleet of two or more nodes can prove a write
  when each follower holds it on disk, and a follower fsync is much
  faster than a storage round trip: a lab fleet measured about 600 ms for
  a bucket proof and about 25 ms for a fleet proof. The bucket upload
  races every fleet proof and either one proves the write, so a slow
  follower cannot make a write slower than a bucket proof. Concurrent
  writes to one cell join one shared upload, so the throughput of one
  cell is not one round trip for each write.
- **A restore is normal work.** Placement handles the restore of an
  inactive cell as ordinary work, and not as an emergency procedure. The
  measured restore times come from the retired external replicator, so this
  page gives no number until a fleet run measures `celld-ltx`.
- **Ten small nodes held real scale.** A fleet of ten nodes, each with 4
  vCPU and 8 GB, held 10,000 resident cells and 20,000 concurrent
  WebSocket connections. We stopped two of the ten nodes, and the data of
  every cell was available again on another node in ~11 s at the tail
  (with reserve headroom).

## The failure edges we intend to find

We must also know where a policy stops, so we record the edges instead of
tuning them away. The clearest edge is the reserve headroom: a fleet that
is full to its resident limit has no space for the cells of a lost node,
so a failure of more than one node at the limit degrades the service,
and a fleet with headroom does not. We measure both sides of that line,
the good restoration with reserve and the red case without, because this
measurement is part of the work.

If you find an edge that we did not find, tell us: a schedule that breaks
a promise, a fault that we did not inject, a number that you cannot
reproduce. That is exactly the bug report that we want:
[github.com/denoland/celld/issues](https://github.com/denoland/celld/issues).

---
name: Release

# One release pipeline, two phases.
#
# A push to the candidate ref builds every native target, attests
# provenance, uploads everything to a DRAFT GitHub release, and
# smoke-builds the container image. Publishing the draft is a separate,
# human-approved step after the candidate binaries pass verification; a
# failed candidate is deleted and main never moves.
#
# Publishing the release (release: published) triggers the container
# phase: architecture images are built from the tagged commit, pushed to
# GHCR, and stitched into a multi-architecture manifest with the same
# provenance attestation as the binaries.
on:
  push:
    branches:
      - candidate
  release:
    types: [published]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: release-${{ github.event_name }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

env:
  RUST_VERSION: 1.97.1
  IMAGE: ghcr.io/denoland/celld

jobs:
  build-celld:
    name: Build celld ${{ matrix.target }}
    if: github.event_name != 'release'
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          - runner: ubuntu-22.04
            target: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
          - runner: ubuntu-22.04-arm
            target: aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
          - runner: macos-14

    timeout-minutes: 90
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6

      - name: Build
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          rustup toolchain install "$RUST_VERSION" --profile minimal
          rustup default "$RUST_VERSION"
          cargo build --release --locked

state.output:
# Security

celld is an alpha. It is not safe for hostile multi-tenant use. Security fixes
apply to the latest release only, so older alpha builds do not receive fixes.

## Security boundary

One fleet runs one application, and celld trusts the application code, the fleet
nodes, and the operators. Application code can use its configured bindings and
can consume shared node resources. Do not run code from mutually distrusting
tenants in one fleet.

celld depends on two external security boundaries:

- A trusted private network protects the internal listener. Use an encrypted
  overlay when the private network does not provide confidentiality.
- Object storage credentials control the fleet. Give each credential access to
  one fleet bucket only.

## Separate the listeners

celld opens two HTTP listeners. The public listener serves the deployed Worker,
and the internal listener serves the peer protocol and the operator API.

Use `--listen` for the public listener. Expose this listener through a load
balancer, a reverse proxy, or a public firewall rule.

Use `--internal-listen` for the internal listener. Its default address is
`127.0.0.1:0`, so celld selects an available loopback port at each start. Use
`--advertise` to give peers an address that reaches this listener.

An explicit advertised address requires an explicit internal-listener address.
celld also rejects an explicit non-loopback public listener without an explicit
internal listener. These checks prevent an obsolete one-listener configuration.

celld cannot verify a hostname or a translated port. You must route the
advertised address to the internal listener, and you must not route it to the
public listener.

The public listener reserves only `/.well-known/celld/health`. A healthy node
returns a 200 response with `{"ok":true}`, and an unhealthy node returns a 503
response. The deployed Worker owns `/health` and every other public path.

The internal listener does not pass an unknown path to the Worker. It returns a
404 response, so an operator request cannot become an application request.

## Protect each surface

| Surface | Required protection |
| --- | --- |
| The public listener | Terminate TLS and authenticate users in a proxy or the application. |
| The internal listener | Restrict access to trusted operators and fleet nodes. Use an encrypted overlay when the private network does not provide confidentiality. |
| The fleet bucket | Restrict the credentials to one fleet bucket. |

The internal listener has three request groups:

- Most operator routes let an operator inspect or control a node without
  request authentication.
- The `/peer/tunnel` route establishes a tunnel for cell fetch, RPC, and
  WebSocket calls. The establishment request carries the fleet HMAC, a clock
  limit, and replay protection, so only a holder of the fleet secret can open
  a tunnel. Each call then crosses inside the tunnel as plain HTTP with the
  cell scope in a reserved header, and these inner calls are not signed.
- The peer-control routes coordinate fleet nodes, and the reserved-cell routes
  access runtime state. These routes use the fleet HMAC for request
  authentication, a clock limit, and replay protection.

All three groups require the trusted private network.

The tunnel permits a request body to stream to the owner, so the fleet HMAC
cannot sign an individual call. The establishment signature decides who can
open a tunnel, and a tunneled call can address an application class or a
runtime class, so every path to a runtime class demands the fleet secret.
The signature does not authenticate the bytes after the establishment, and
it does not encrypt any traffic. The private network must therefore stay
trusted, and the fleet HMAC does not replace this network boundary.

celld does not terminate TLS on either listener. Do not expose the internal
listener to the public internet. Use an encrypted overlay such as WireGuard or
Tailscale when the network does not provide the required confidentiality.
=====TELEM
# Telemetry

celld can record traces and logs for the requests it serves. The
feature is off by default, and the off state costs nothing. Set
`CELLD_OTEL=1` to turn it on.

The default sink is the fleet bucket. celld writes Parquet files under
the `telemetry/` prefix, so a fleet with a bucket has observability
with no other service. DuckDB can query these files directly. An
alternative sink sends the same data to an OpenTelemetry collector.

The schema is version `v0-unstable`. The column names can change
before a stable release, and each file carries the schema version in
its object metadata.

## Configuration

| variable | default | effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CELLD_OTEL` | `0` | Set this value to `1` to enable telemetry. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_SINK` | `bucket` | `bucket` writes Parquet to the fleet bucket. `otlp` sends OTLP/HTTP protobuf to a collector instead. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_BUCKET` | the fleet bucket | A different bucket for the Parquet files, on the same endpoint and credentials. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_RETENTION` | `30d` | celld deletes telemetry files older than this. `none` disables the deletion, so your own lifecycle rules can control the data. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_MS` | `300000` | celld writes a Parquet file after this many milliseconds of buffered events. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_BYTES` | `5242880` | celld writes a Parquet file after the buffered events reach this many bytes. celld uses the limit it reaches first. |
| `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER` | `parentbased_always_on` | A standard sampler name. `traceidratio` with `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG` records a fraction of the traces. |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | `http://localhost:4318` | The collector base URL, for the `otlp` sink. `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` and `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT` also apply. |
| `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` | `celld` | The service name in the exported resource. |

The `bucket` sink requires the node to have a fleet bucket
(`CELLD_BUCKET`). The `otlp` sink works on a node without one.

## What celld records

celld records a span for each request a stateless Worker serves, for
each event a cell serves (a fetch, an alarm, an RPC, a WebSocket
message), for each outbound `fetch()`, and for each cell start. A
span carries the request id, the cell, the isolate, the
queue wait, the outbound URL and status, and the durability facts the
runtime already knows.

celld also records each `console.log` line as a log record. The log
record carries the trace id and the span id of the handler that wrote
it, so a query can join the logs to the traces. The correlation
survives `await`.

celld reads the W3C `traceparent` header on incoming requests, so its
spans join the trace of the system in front of it. celld sends a
`traceparent` header on outbound `fetch()`, so downstream systems can
join too. A Worker call to a Durable Object stays in one trace.

# Rust library API

## Select facade

Use `celld::asyncrt::select!` when the source order must not decide a tie. The
macro selects a cyclic start for each poll, and it rejects the `biased;` token.

Use `celld::asyncrt::select_biased!` only when the source order defines the
winner of a tie. The macro polls the branches in source order. The first token
must be a non-empty string literal that states which arm wins and why.

## Durability ownership

The `celld` crate requires one `node_log::DurabilityOwner` for each local
durability stack. The owner keeps the coupled registration. It retains each
live or failed background-task handle until shutdown joins it. It also retains
each admitted release-close task and the final close handle until the
registered managed databases close.

The crate removes these public functions:

- `LtxRepl::set_shipper`
- `LtxRepl::set_bundle_sink`
- `node_log::spawn_maintenance`
- `node_log::spawn_fragment_gc`

The old setter functions installed separate strong references. A
`NodeLogManager` also retains its `LtxRepl`, so these references can create an
ownership cycle.

The old spawn functions detached their task handles. An embedding process
therefore cannot stop or join the tasks during local shutdown.

Construct a `DurabilityOwner` after the node-log recovery completes. Call
`DurabilityOwner::start_background` before the process starts its application
services, and retain the owner for the process lifetime.

Await `LtxRepl::release` when a runtime stops a cell and keeps its local files.
The method admits a managed database close to the owner task group before it
waits. Require an `Ok` result before another activation reuses the local path.

With this I've grasped the overall picture of the repo. Time to design the page plan (taxonomy).

Repository: celld — self-hosted distributed Durable Objects. Three crates:
- crates/logic — pure sans-IO decision-making core (State, Event, Effect, on_event).
- crates/celld — the daemon: effect execution + adapters (V8, tokio, object store, HTTP listener, CLI).
- crates/ltx — vendored SQLite→object store LTX replication (Litestream re-implementation).

---
type: architecture
title: "Execution Boundary and Actor Model"
description: "How the celld binary separates the serial Actor execution domain from ambient-effect adapters: the on_event loop, asyncrt as the sole ambient-prism facade, the clippy boundary lint, and the cfg-gated simulated asyncrt used by deterministic tests."
tags: [architecture, actor, asyncrt, clippy, deterministic-simulation, v8]
---

## The one-actor rule

`crates/celld` is the effect executor. Its crate doc states the invariant the
rest of the boundary exists to protect: the executable owns **one serial actor
which is the only caller of `celld_logic::on_event`**, and adapter futures
never borrow core state — they send versioned completion events back through
the actor's mailbox (`crates/celld/lib.rs:4-9`). `actor.rs` calls itself "the
serial lifecycle executor and its shell-side request drivers"
(`crates/celld/actor.rs:3`).

The actor holds `celld_logic::State` plus executor-local bookkeeping maps
(pending request replies, handoff waiters, durability waiters, gated
responses) (`crates/celld/actor.rs:1728-1790`). Every input — a mailbox
`Message`, a completed effect, or a fired timer — is exactly one
`ActorInput`, and `Actor::step` turns it into one or more core `Event`s fed
through `drive`, which calls the core and translates each returned `Effect`
into a future or timer arm collected in a `StepOutput`
(`crates/celld/actor.rs:1095-1130, 2171-2260, 2743-2785`).

## The production select loop

The production selector (`Actor::run`, in `actor/production.rs`) is a
start/select/step loop over three sources: the mailbox receiver, a
`FuturesUnordered` of in-flight effect futures, and a `DelayQueue` of timer
arms (`crates/celld/actor/production.rs:9-44`). The selector deliberately
stays **unbiased**: production permits any ready-input order, and direct
callers can use `Actor::start` and `Actor::step` without the raw loop.

Timer arms implement a displacement discipline shared with the deterministic
tests: each `TimerArm` carries a per-slot ordinal, `TimerSlots::arm` assigns
it and reports the displaced value, and a late `install` removes the stale
`DelayQueue` entry (`crates/celld/actor.rs:66-128, 1108-1130`). Timer slots
coalesce — newest arming wins — **except** `OperationDeadline`, keyed by
`OpId`, and `QueuedActivation`, keyed by cell and generation, because a
shared slot would silently cancel an earlier deadline while its operation is
still outstanding (`crates/celld/actor.rs:38-53`).

## asyncrt: the only holder of ambient primitives

`crates/celld/asyncrt.rs` "owns the ambient production primitives which the
boundary lint prohibits elsewhere" (`crates/celld/asyncrt.rs:3-4`). It exposes
the tokio-backed facades the rest of the engine uses: `spawn`/`blocking`/
`block_on`, `sleep`/`sleep_until`/`timeout`/`interval`, `wall_ms`/`mono_ms`/
`mono_us` clocks, a labeled `rng(consumer)` stream, `process_tag`, and the
injected filesystem handle `fs()` (`crates/celld/asyncrt.rs:110-311`). The
module doc adds the key extensibility fact: *"A cfg-gated build can replace
this module with another execution backend"*
(`crates/celld/asyncrt.rs:9-11`).

Two select macros come out of this facade. `celld::asyncrt::select!` is an
unbiased select whose per-poll branch order is chosen by a process-wide,
`OsRng`-seeded cyclic counter (`select_start`, `crates/celld/asyncrt.rs:170-187`);
`select_biased!` requires a non-empty string literal as its first token
stating which arm wins and why (`crates/celld/lib.rs:42-58`,
`crates/celld/main.rs:8-21`). The macro implementation is adapted from Tokio
1.53.1's internal `select.rs` over re-exported `doc(hidden)` items, so a
Tokio version bump is expected to fail loudly at compile time rather than
silently; the in-tree comment records that a narrowed tokio constraint was
considered and rejected (`crates/celld/lib.rs:12-29`).

## How the lint enforces the boundary

`clippy.toml` (workspace root) forbids, by path, the ambient calls inside the
execution boundary: `tokio::spawn`/`spawn_blocking`, `tokio::time::*`,
`std::time::SystemTime::now`/`Instant::now`, `rand::random`,
`std::process::id`, and the whole `std::fs`/`tokio::fs`/`Path` metadata
surface, each with a `reason` pointing at the `asyncrt` or injected-filesystem
replacement. The macro lint bans `tokio::select` in favor of the domain
macros, and `println!`/`print!` in favor of `celld::cli_output::Output` and
`note!`; `rand::rngs::OsRng` is a disallowed *type* (`clippy.toml:1-49,
55-86`). The `celld` and `celld-ltx` packages set `disallowed_macros =
"forbid"` in their `[lints.clippy]` sections, so no module-level attribute
can lower the macro policy (`crates/celld/Cargo.toml:19-21`,
`crates/ltx/Cargo.toml:24-27`); `crates/celld/lib.rs:3` additionally warns
`disallowed_methods`/`disallowed_types` crate-wide. Modules that legitimately
sit outside the boundary carry an explicit `#[allow]` or a header comment
instead of silently bypassing the lint.

The decision core itself needs no lint: `celld-logic` declares *"Pure
decision core: no async, I/O, clocks, randomness, locks, or dependencies"*
and ships with no dependencies at all (`crates/logic/Cargo.toml:5-16`).

## Who is inside and who is outside

Module headers partition the binary. These modules state they execute
*outside* the Actor execution domain: `assets.rs`, `control_plane.rs`,
`deploy.rs`, `fleet.rs`, `js.rs`, `peer_probe.rs`, `pool.rs`, `storage.rs`,
`ws_client.rs` — for example, `storage.rs` calls itself "V8-thread SQLite
plumbing outside the Actor execution domain" (`crates/celld/storage.rs:2-3`).
`runtime.rs` (the V8 cell-host arm) keeps "its executor and observability
clocks ambient" (`crates/celld/runtime.rs:2-3`), and `js.rs` notes that the
raw V8 adapter and its child modules stay outside the domain while the
Actor-reachable wake and WebSocket state is injected through `HostServices`
(`crates/celld/js.rs:2-5`). `host_services.rs` is the seam that makes this
work in simulation: production installs one service set, a deterministic
domain installs one set per simulated node, so co-hosted incarnations do not
share counters or host measurements (`crates/celld/host_services.rs:3-8`).
The binary header summarizes the split: "The binary contains connection,
startup, shutdown, and V8 shell code. The library Actor owns the execution
domain and its routed adapters." (`crates/celld/main.rs:2-4`).

The practical consequence for maintenance: new code that decides behavior
goes into `celld-logic` as a pure predicate; new code that touches sockets,
timers, or the filesystem either lives in an adapter module with its ambient
calls allowed, or runs inside the actor and goes through `asyncrt` so a
simulated build can substitute it.

## cfg-gated worlds for deterministic testing

Production correctness tests are compiled behind
`#[cfg(celld_internal_tests)]` gates that `include!` **external corpus files
whose paths arrive through environment variables**: `CELLD_INTERNAL_ASYNCRT`
replaces `asyncrt` with the simulated runtime, and
`CELLD_INTERNAL_ASYNCRT_TESTS`, `CELLD_CONFORMANCE_WORLD_TESTS`,
`CELLD_CONFORMANCE_WORLD_S1/S2/S3/S5A/S5B/S5C_TESTS`,
`CELLD_CONFORMANCE_CORE_LOOP_TESTS`, `CELLD_CONFORMANCE_O3_ORACLE_TESTS`,
`CELLD_CONFORMANCE_WORLD_COVERAGE_TESTS`, `CELLD_CONFORMANCE_SIM_STORE_TESTS`,
`CELLD_CONFORMANCE_SIM_CELL_HOST_TESTS`, and `CELLD_INTERNAL_SQLITE_FAULT`
mount the simulation store, cell host, world suites, oracle, and an
SQLite fault injector (`crates/celld/lib.rs:299-435`). The corpus files
themselves are not in this repository: a plain checkout contains the gates
and the real `asyncrt`, not the simulated world, so a contributor sees these
suites compile-fail or vanish unless the harness supplies the env paths. The
gate on the simulated `asyncrt` is the flag alone — *not* `test` — because a
dependency never has `test` set, and the external harness binary must see the
same simulated world the in-crate suites see
(`crates/celld/lib.rs:306-317`). `cargo` also knows the flag is intentional
via `check-cfg = ["cfg(celld_internal_tests)"]` in each crate's lints
(`crates/celld/Cargo.toml:15-16`, `crates/logic/Cargo.toml:13-15`).

## Uncertainty

The in-tree code proves the *seam* (a flag-selected simulated backend
exists), but the content of the deterministic world lives in the external
corpus referenced by the `env!` paths; this wiki does not describe its
behavior beyond what `docs/testing.md` states and the gates show.

## See also

- `openwiki/architecture/logic-decision-core.md` — the pure core this
  boundary protects.
- `openwiki/concepts/js-runtime-and-apis.md` — the V8 arm's side of the
  split.
- `openwiki/testing/testing-strategy.md` — how simulation and conformance
  suites use these gates.

claims.statement: The celld binary runs one serial Actor that is the only caller of celld_logic::on_event; adapter futures never borrow core state and return versioned completion events through the actor mailbox.

The production Actor::run loop selects unbiasedly over three sources — mailbox receiver, FuturesUnordered of in-flight effect futures, and a DelayQueue of timer arms — feeding each ready input into exactly one Actor::step.

One ActorInput (Message, Completed, or TimerFired) drives one or more core Events through Actor::drive, which calls the decision core and translates each returned Effect into an executor future or timer arm collected in StepOutput.

Timer arms use a shared displacement discipline: most slots coalesce to the newest arm via per-slot ordinals, but OperationDeadline (keyed by OpId) and QueuedActivation (keyed by cell+generation) never coalesce because a shared slot would silently cancel an outstanding operation's deadline.

crates/celld/asyncrt.rs owns the ambient production primitives (tokio task spawning, timers, wall/monotonic clocks, RNG, process values, filesystem handle) that the boundary lint prohibits elsewhere, and a cfg-gated build replaces the entire module with another execution backend.

The asyncrt facade exposes spawn/blocking/block_on, sleep/sleep_until/timeout/interval built on mono_ms deadlines, wall_ms, labeled rng streams, process_tag, and the injected celld_ltx::FileSystem handle fs().

celld::asyncrt::select! randomizes branch poll order with a process-wide OsRng-seeded cyclic counter (select_start), select! compile-errors on a `biased;` token, and select_biased! requires a non-empty string literal stating which arm wins and why.

Workspace clippy.toml forbids raw tokio spawn/sleep/timeout calls, std clocks, rand::random, std::process::id, and the std::fs/tokio::fs surface, and bans the tokio::select, println!/print! macros and the OsRng type; celld and celld-ltx set disallowed_macros = forbid so no module attribute can lower the macro policy.

The celld-logic crate declares itself a pure decision core with no async, I/O, clocks, randomness, or locks and carries zero dependencies, so the boundary rule there is structural rather than lint-enforced.

Module headers partition the binary: the raw V8 adapter (js.rs), SQLite plumbing (storage.rs), and V8 cell-host runtime keep ambient clocks and run outside the Actor execution domain, while the library Actor owns the domain and its routed adapters and the binary holds connection/startup/shutdown/V8 shell code.

HostServices is the injection seam for process-visible services: production installs one service set and a deterministic domain installs one set per simulated node so co-hosted incarnations do not share counters or host measurements.

Deterministic-test worlds are mounted behind cfg(celld_internal_tests) with include!(env!(...)) gates that pull external corpus files (simulated asyncrt, conformance world/core-loop/sim-store/sim-cell-host suites, oracle, SQLite fault injector) named only by environment variables, so a plain checkout contains the gates but not the corpus.

The simulated asyncrt is gated on the celld_internal_tests flag alone and not on test, because dependencies never see cfg(test) and the external engine-test harness binary must observe the same simulated world as the in-crate suites.

Excellent material. I'll write the page now.

Page: openwiki/architecture/logic-decision-core.md

Outline:
- Purpose: pure sans-IO core; on_event as the sole transition; State/Event/Effect.
- Vocabulary module (types.rs): Event is the sole input, Effect is the sole output; data only.
- on_event: monotonic clock merge (max of event stamps); large match; all async Effect carries an op: OpId; stale completions are ignored (per doc comment in types.rs).
- State: what is held (cells map, phase machine, barriers, permits, capacity waiters, reservations); draining/sticky.
- Phase state machine: cold start Inactive → WaitingActivation → ReadingOwner → (RecoveringOwnerLog lease-fold) → Acquiring → Restoring → Starting → Publishing → Resident/EnsuringDurability → Cleaning/Dormant; celld eviction vs Cloudflare eviction semantics.
- Output gate: Channel enum enumerates all egress paths; core does not read the channel; one rule per barrier map; CELOUT... bypass when CELLD_OUTPUT_GATE=0 (shell sends no Event::Output at all).
- Module layout by policy area: quote the module headers.
- Fences inside the core: cell scope character set is a security fence (cell.rs), http authority (http.rs), peer identity (peer.rs).
- Log tiers: log_tier decisions are in the core, node_log is the executor; log_evict gray followers.
- Where it's enforced: zero dependencies, Cargo comment.
- How to verify: deterministic simulation drives the core (see testing page).

Claims (about 12):
1. on_event is the sole entry point for behavioral state; both the executor and the simulator supply events and execute effects; adapters never mutate State (lib.rs#L3-L8).
2. types.rs: Event is the sole input, Effect is the sole output, "no decisions are made here" (types.rs#L2-L7).
3. All async effects carry an OpId version, and completions with a stale op are ignored (types.rs#L737-L740 comment).
4. on_event advances the internal clock as the max of the event's monotonic timestamp (lib.rs#L5215-L5223).
5. State fields include the cell table and explicit permit sets: activation_permits, eviction_permits, capacity_waiters FIFO as the whole admission policy to prevent starvation (lib.rs#L487-L560).
6. Phase machine enumerates cold-start path including lease-fold takeover interlock RecoveringOwnerLog and EnsuringDurability; celld evict = Dormant, publish = shedding (lib.rs#L100-L170).

input.content:
---
type: architecture
title: "Logic Decision Core"
description: "The pure sans-IO celld-logic crate: State/Event/Effect vocabulary, on_event as the sole state transition, the cell Phase state machine, the single output-gate choke point, security-fence predicates, and the module-per-policy layout."
tags: [architecture, sans-io, state-machine, output-gate, fencing]
---

## What the core is

`crates/logic` (`celld-logic`) is the clean-sheet decision core: *"on_event is
the only way behavioral state advances. The production executor and
deterministic simulator both feed it events and perform the returned effects.
No adapter may mutate State directly."* (`crates/logic/lib.rs:3-8`). Purity is
structural, not a convention to remember: the crate declares *"no async, I/O,
clocks, randomness, locks, or dependencies"* and its `Cargo.toml` carries no
`[dependencies]` at all (`crates/logic/Cargo.toml:8-11`).

## The vocabulary: Event in, Effect out

`types.rs` is data only — "`Event` is the only way in, `Effect` the only way
out, and the rest are the shapes those two carry. No decision is made in this
file — that is `State` in the crate root" (`crates/logic/types.rs:3-8`). Two
properties of this contract carry the distributed correctness:

- **Every asynchronous effect is versioned.** `Effect` carries an `OpId` per
  operation, and "completion events with an obsolete `op` are ignored"
  (`crates/logic/types.rs:737-740`) — the core can never be confused by a
  late answer from an effect it already superseded.
- **Time enters through events.** `on_event` folds each event's `now_ms` /
  `now_mono_ms` stamps into `State` with `max`, so the core's clock cannot
  go backwards even if the executor delivers stamps out of order
  (`crates/logic/lib.rs:5215-5223`). Many events also carry the monotonic
  instant alongside wall time (e.g. `StartNodeLease` anchors the first TTL
  on `now_mono_ms` so a slow boot does not consume the lease)
  (`crates/logic/types.rs:402-412`).

`State` is the whole authoritative coordination picture: the node lease
authority, the cell table keyed by `CellId`, request indexes, activation and
eviction permit sets, a FIFO `capacity_waiters` queue ("FIFO is the whole
admission policy ... a waiter with `k` waiters ahead of it is admitted within
`k` releases"), load reservations, and the output-gate barrier map
(`crates/logic/lib.rs:487-560`). Making permits explicit sets rather than
inferring them from executor tasks keeps "the bound part of the replayable
state machine" (`crates/logic/lib.rs:534-547`).

## The cell Phase machine

`Phase` (`crates/logic/lib.rs:105-170`) enumerates the cold-to-resident
lifecycle: `Inactive → WaitingActivation → ReadingOwner → (ReadingNodeLease |
RecoveringOwnerLog) → Acquiring → Restoring → Starting → Publishing →
Resident`, with `EnsuringDurability`, `Cleaning`, and `Dormant` on the exit
side. Two entries encode protocol subtleties:

- `RecoveringOwnerLog` is the takeover interlock (lease-fold): a dead
  owner's unsealed folded log state must be recovered before the cell may be
  claimed (`crates/logic/lib.rs:121-126`).
- The celld/Cloudflare vocabulary divergence is stated in the code: celld
  "evicts" a cell *out of memory* producing `Dormant`, and **shedding** is
  what publishes it unowned, while Cloudflare's "evict" means off-host
  (`crates/logic/lib.rs:106-110`).

Admission distinguishes capacity from overload exactly once: `has_capacity`
checks the hard residency count (`occupied_below(max_resident)` — "known
exactly and counted -- never sampled") and the shedding latch; the only
sampled fact that refuses admission is genuine memory pressure
(`crates/logic/lib.rs:1369-1377`).

## The output gate: one choke point

The core holds the single durability rule for egress: *"Nothing that reveals
a cell's state may leave this process while that cell has a write it cannot
prove durable"* (`crates/logic/output_gate.rs:4-10`). `Channel` enumerates
every revealing route — response, outbound `fetch`, hibernatable WebSocket
frame, self-polled socket, service binding, cell RPC, queue batch — with the
`WsSelf` exception explained (a frame the handler may itself be awaiting
cannot be captured, so it waits on a durability ticket instead)
(`crates/logic/types.rs:335-365`). The implementation contract is explicit:
the shell holds each effect and sends an `Event::Output`; the core applies
*one* rule to every route and echoes the same `Channel` back in
`Effect::Release` — **the core does not match on the channel**, because
per-channel logic would "split the invariant into six independent rules"
(`crates/logic/output_gate.rs:12-31`). With `CELLD_OUTPUT_GATE=0` the shell
simply sends no `Event::Output`, bypassing the gate without a second rule
(`crates/logic/output_gate.rs:23-26`). An earlier split implementation (core
reader gate + shell WebSocket queue + in-handler check) is what motivated the
single barrier map (`crates/logic/output_gate.rs:33-38`).

The `State::barriers` map ties gate entries to durability ops: "an open gate
makes its cell active, so the cell cannot be evicted underneath it"
(`crates/logic/lib.rs:509-515`).

## Fencing decisions live in the core too

`fence()` drains the gate atomically with the loss of authority: gated
outputs are released with `Err(RequestError::NodeFenced)` so "a write is
never acknowledged after the node loses authority" (`crates/logic/lib.rs:5076-5100`);
a node-level lease expiry routes through `fence_node`, which additionally
emits `Effect::Halt { code: 3, reason: HaltReason::NodeLeaseExpired }`
(`crates/logic/lib.rs:2810-2815`). Alarm gates are the deliberate exception:
an alarm has no output to fail and is left in the bucket for the next owner
to rediscover (`crates/logic/lib.rs:5090-5098`).

## Security fences as pure predicates

Three input-validation policies are marked **SECURITY fence** in their module
headers, all as pure functions so simulation can cover them exhaustively:

- `cell.rs`: cell-scope charset, because the scope is interpolated into a
  path and an object key (`crates/logic/cell.rs:1-8`);
- `peer.rs`: peer identity shape, signature clock window, and replay-cache
  retention (`crates/logic/peer.rs:3-8`);
- `http.rs`: request-authority shape, because the header is client-controlled
  when no proxy sits in front (`crates/logic/http.rs:3-8`).

## Module-per-policy layout

The remaining modules each reify one policy area with its executor named in
the header — representative examples:

| module | decision | named executor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `gate.rs` | per-cell input-gate concurrency safety | actor event dispatch |
| `isolate.rs` + `schedule.rs` | isolate pool and per-isolate dispatch | `js.rs` run loop + pool |
| `restore.rs` | newest-safe restore source; availability is I/O | activation |
| `wake.rs` | alarm-wake entry reconciliation + key scheme | async S3 flusher |
| `queue.rs` / `kv.rs` | queue/namespace bounds, leases, addresses | reserved cells |
| `alarm.rs` / `cron.rs` | retry backoff / next-occurrence math | SQLite rows |
| `log_tier.rs` / `log_evict.rs` | ensemble membership, gray-follower eviction | `node_log.rs` |
| `pressure.rs` | shedding classifier (hysteresis latch) | `main.rs` edge sampling |
| `drain.rs` | fleet drain-token claims | `drain_token.rs` |
| `routing.rs` | whether a failed peer dispatch may be retried | shell dispatch |
| `dead_node_reconciliation.rs` | retire legacy `node-cells/` debris | `dead_node_gc.rs` |

(Module headers: `crates/logic/gate.rs:1-8`, `crates/logic/restore.rs:1-8`,
`crates/logic/wake.rs:1-8`, `crates/logic/log_evict.rs:1-8`,
`crates/logic/routing.rs:1-8`, `crates/logic/alarm.rs:1-6`,
`crates/logic/cron.rs:1-8`, `crates/logic/queue.rs:1-10`,
`crates/logic/drain.rs:1-8`, `crates/logic/isolate.rs:1-8`,
`crates/logic/dead_node_reconciliation.rs:1-6`.)

`on_event` itself (`crates/logic/lib.rs:5215+`) is the dispatcher: it stamps
the monotonic clock, then routes each `Event` variant to a `State` method
(`start_node_lease`, `timer_fired`, `request`, `node_lease_cas_completed`,
…), returning the accumulated `Vec<Effect>` to the caller.

## See also

- `openwiki/architecture/execution-boundary.md` — the actor that owns the
  only `on_event` call site and executes the effects.
- `openwiki/concepts/durability-and-replication.md` — what a durability
  proof actually is.
- `openwiki/testing/testing-strategy.md` — driving this core under seeded
  adversarial schedules.

claims.statement: In celld-logic, on_event is the only way behavioral state advances; the production executor and the deterministic simulator both feed it events and perform the returned effects, and no adapter may mutate State directly.
types.rs is pure vocabulary: Event is the only input, Effect the only output, and all decisions live in State at the crate root.
Every asynchronous Effect is versioned with an OpId, and completion events carrying an obsolete op are ignored, so late executor answers cannot corrupt the core's lifecycle state.
on_event advances the core's clocks only by folding each event's now_ms/now_mono_ms stamps with max, so time in the decision core cannot run backwards regardless of executor delivery order.

State keeps activation and eviction permits as explicit cell sets and capacity waiters as a FIFO queue, making admission bounds part of the replayable state machine; FIFO is the whole admission policy and bounds each waiter's wait by the number of arrivals ahead of it.

The Phase state machine enumerates the cold-to-resident lifecycle including the RecoveringOwnerLog lease-fold takeover interlock and EnsuringDurability, and the header states celld 'evicts' out of memory into Dormant while shedding publishes unowned.
has_capacity treats residency as a hard exact count (never sampled) and lets only the memory-pressure shedding latch additionally refuse admission.

The output gate holds any egress that reveals cell state until its write is proven durable; the Channel enum enumerates every revealing route, the core applies one rule without matching on the channel, and it returns the same channel in Effect::Release.
Disabling the gate with CELLD_OUTPUT_GATE=0 is done in the shell by not sending Event::Output at all, so the core keeps exactly one durability rule.

Fencing is atomic with gate failure: State::fence drains every held output gate entry to Err(NodeFenced) so no write is acknowledged after the node loses authority, while alarm gates are released without output and left for the next owner to rediscover.
Node-lease loss routes through fence_node, which fences the cell state and emits Effect::Halt with code 3 and HaltReason::NodeLeaseExpired to the executor.

Cell-scope charset, peer-authentication predicates, and HTTP authority-shape checks are declared SECURITY fences and implemented as pure sans-IO predicates because their values are interpolated into object keys, authorization decisions, and request.url.
celld-logic enforces purity structurally: it declares no async, I/O, clocks, randomness, locks, or dependencies and its manifest carries no dependencies section.

---
type: architecture
title: "Architecture Overview"
description: "The celld workspace: three crates with a strict dependency direction — a pure decision core (celld-logic), the daemon/executor host (celld), and a vendored SQLite-to-object-store replication engine (celld-ltx) — plus the build profiles and pinned dependencies that shape the design."
tags: [architecture, workspace, crates, dependencies, build-profiles]
---

## What celld is

celld is a self-hosted daemon that runs Cloudflare Workers and Durable
Objects code on your own machines. Each object is a **cell** — a named
server with its own private SQLite database. A **node** is one `celld`
process, and the nodes that share one object-storage bucket form a
**fleet**: ownership of a cell is decided by a conditional bucket write,
there is no consensus service, and committed SQLite writes are replicated
as LTX data so acknowledged data survives node loss (RPO=0)
(`README.md:3-34`).

## The three-crate split

The workspace manifest opens by stating the rule the layout enforces:
*"Clean-sheet celld workspace. `crates/logic` owns all behavioral state and
decisions; `crates/celld` is only an effect executor and adapter host"*
(`Cargo.toml:1-5`). Dependency direction is strictly one way:

```
celld (daemon: V8 host, HTTP, CLI, effects)
 ├─→ celld-logic  (pure sans-IO decision core; zero dependencies)
 └─→ celld-ltx    (vendored SQLite WAL → object-store replication)
```

- **`celld-logic`** is the behavioral brain: `State`, `Event`, `Effect`,
  `on_event` as the only state transition, plus one module per policy
  (routing, gates, pressure, restore, wake, queue, alarm, cron, kv,
  isolate, log tier). See `openwiki/architecture/logic-decision-core.md`.
- **`celld`** is a library plus one binary (`[lib] path = "lib.rs"`,
  `[[bin]] name = "celld" path = "main.rs"`). It embeds V8 (`v8 = "152.1"`),
  runs the serial Actor that is the sole caller of `on_event`, and provides
  the listeners, CLI subcommands (`deploy`, `dev`, `diagnose`, `cell`,
  `d1`, `kv`, `queue`, …), object-store adapters, telemetry, and the JS API
  (`crates/celld/Cargo.toml:11-15`). The boundary mechanics are covered in
  `openwiki/architecture/execution-boundary.md`.
- **`celld-ltx`** is an embedded replication engine: *"in-process
  SQLite→object-store replication for celld"*, vendored on 2026-08-03 from
  rustyriver — itself a Rust reimplementation of Litestream v0.5 and the
  LTX format — and *"celld owns and evolves this snapshot; it does not
  track an upstream branch"*. It exists to serve celld's RPO=0 durability
  goal for every cell write (`crates/ltx/Cargo.toml:1-8`).

Notably, `celld-ltx` does **not** depend on `celld-logic`: replication is
mechanical storage work, and the durability *policy* stays in the core. The
LTX and logic crates are joined in `celld` by `ltx_repl.rs` (the in-process
backend) and executed under decisions from `celld_logic::log_tier` etc.
(`crates/celld/ltx_repl.rs:3-9`).

## Ownership of the big subsystems

`crates/celld` is a flat module list; the meaningful grouping is by job:

| Subsystem | Modules | Detail page |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Execution domain | `actor.rs`, `asyncrt.rs`, `host_services.rs` | execution-boundary.md |
| Decisions | (all of `celld-logic`) | logic-decision-core.md |
| V8 runtime & JS APIs | `runtime.rs`, `js.rs` + `js/`, `pool.rs`, `storage.rs` | js-runtime-and-apis.md |
| Durability path | `ltx_repl.rs`, `replication.rs`, `node_log.rs` | durability-and-replication.md |
| Fleet coordination | `fleet.rs`, `ownership_store.rs`, `drain_token.rs`, `dead_node_gc.rs`, `wake.rs` | cells-and-ownership.md |
| Networking | `main.rs` (listeners), `main/peer_tunnel.rs`, `main/websocket.rs`, `peer_auth.rs`, `ws_client.rs`, `protocol.rs` | http-routing-and-peer-tunnel.md |
| Application lifecycle | `deploy.rs`, `generation.rs`, `assets.rs`, `dev.rs`, `local_store.rs` | deployments-and-dev.md |
| Object storage | `bucket.rs` (+ ltx `client/`) | object-storage.md |
| Cell-backed services | reserved classes via `logic::queue/kv/cron/alarm/wake`, `operator_cell.rs` | cell-services.md |
| Operations | `machine.rs`, `memory.rs`, `cli_options.rs`, `env_vars.rs`, `startup.rs`, `cell_cli.rs`, `d1_cli.rs`, `kv_cli.rs`, `queue_cli.rs`, `peer_probe.rs`, `control_plane.rs` | fleet-operations.md |
| Observability | `telemetry.rs`, `otlp.rs` | observability-and-telemetry.md |

`main.rs` states the binary/library split: *"The binary contains
connection, startup, shutdown, and V8 shell code. The library Actor owns
the execution domain and its routed adapters"* (`crates/celld/main.rs:2-4`).

## Build-shape decisions

- **Every direct dependency is declared once** in `[workspace.dependencies]`
  "so the crates can never drift onto two versions of the same crate;
  members add their own features" (`Cargo.toml:33-35`). `rusqlite` alignment
  is a hard constraint: `libsqlite3-sys` carries `links="sqlite3"`, so the
  workspace physically cannot hold two versions
  (`crates/ltx/Cargo.toml:36-38`).
- **Release is size-tuned**: fat LTO, `codegen-units = 1`, `opt-level =
  "s"` (not `"z"` — measure RPS before trading further), `panic = "abort"`
  to drop unwind tables, `strip = true` (`Cargo.toml:7-14`).
- **A second profile, `lab`**, is the fast experiment loop: release
  optimization minus the fat-LTO relink (`lto = "thin"`,
  `codegen-units = 16`, incremental) and *unstripped with line tables* so
  `perf` on a node attributes CPU by function; shipped artifacts stay on
  `release` (`Cargo.toml:16-27`).
- **Pins encode architectural decisions.** `fastwebsockets` is pinned to
  `=0.8.1` for the unstable `unstable-split` feature, because a WebSocket
  read is not cancel-safe and the tunnel needs independent read/write
  halves; the comment records that celld carries that risk knowingly
  (`Cargo.toml:50-59`). `sqlite-vec` is pinned `=0.1.9` to the audited C
  amalgamation (pre-v1 binding outside compatibility policy)
  (`Cargo.toml:116-118`). `v8 = "152.1"` is the first rusty_v8 carrying
  `v8::Locker` and `Send` `Globals`, which shared isolates need — the
  comment records the upstream issues (`Cargo.toml:136-140`).
- jemalloc with stats is the allocator, because the pressure classifier
  needs `stats.allocated` vs `stats.resident` — the pages the allocator
  keeps but no cell uses (`Cargo.toml:122-127`).

## Where to go next

- Reading order for behavior changes: `logic-decision-core.md` →
  `execution-boundary.md` → the relevant concept page.
- Operating the result: `openwiki/operations/fleet-operations.md`.
- How correctness is argued: `openwiki/testing/testing-strategy.md`.

parts.text:
From here, I'll submit the claims for the overview page. Claims:

1. Splitting the workspace: logic owns all behavioral state and decisions, while celld is only an effect executor and adapter host (Cargo.toml#L1-L5).
2. Dependency direction: celld depends on celld-logic and celld-ltx, whereas ltx depends on neither logic nor celld (crates/celld/Cargo.toml#L34-L36, crates/ltx/Cargo.toml#L34-L47, crates/logic/Cargo.toml#L8-L11).
3. ltx is a vendored 2026-08-03 snapshot of rustyriver (a port of Litestream v0.5 + LTX), and celld manages its evolution independently of upstream (crates/ltx/Cargo.toml#L1-L8).
4. The celld crate = one lib and a single binary "celld" (crates/celld/Cargo.toml#L9-L14).
5. All direct dependencies are hoisted up to workspace.dependencies to prevent version drift (Cargo.toml#L33-L35).
6. Because of libsqlite3-sys's links="sqlite3", rusqlite has to match across the entire workspace (crates/ltx/Cargo.toml#L36-L38 + Cargo.toml#L110).
7. The release profile is tuned for size (fat LTO, cgu 1, opt-s, panic=abort, strip). The lab profile is for fast iteration and for perf attribution via symbols (Cargo.toml#L7-L27).
8. fastwebsockets is strictly pinned to =0.8.1 with unstable-split for the safety of non-cancel-safe WS reads. The risk is explicitly acknowledged (Cargo.toml#L50-L59).
9. v8 = 152.1 is the first rusty_v8 with v8::Locker and Send Globals for shared isolates (Cargo.toml#L136-L140).
10. sqlite-vec is strictly pinned to the audited amalgamation (Cargo.toml#L116-L118).
11. jemalloc stats support: because the pressure classifier needs the diff of allocated vs resident (Cargo.toml#L122-L127).
12. Binary/library split comment (crates/celld/main.rs#L2-L4).

Evidence lines: Cargo.toml L33-35 "# Every direct dependency lives here..." — verify: line 33 is a comment, lines 34-35 are the same. From the earlier reading: line 33 "# Every direct dependency lives here so the crates can never drift onto two", 34 "# versions of the same crate; members add their own features.", 35 [workspace.dependencies]. Good.

The celld Cargo.toml dependency lines: celld-logic.workspace = true is line 34, celld-ltx is line 35. No problem (L34-L36).

claims.statement: The celld workspace is a clean-sheet split in which crates/logic owns all behavioral state and decisions and crates/celld is only an effect executor and adapter host.
Dependency direction is one-way: celld depends on celld-logic and celld-ltx; celld-ltx depends on tokio/rusqlite/object_store but on neither celld crate; celld-logic has zero dependencies.

celld-ltx is a snapshot vendored 2026-08-03 from rustyriver (a Rust reimplementation of Litestream v0.5 and the LTX format); celld owns and evolves the snapshot and does not track an upstream branch, and it exists to serve celld's RPO=0 durability goal for every cell write.
The celld package is one library (lib.rs) plus one binary named celld (main.rs).
The celld binary holds connection, startup, shutdown, and V8 shell code, while the library Actor owns the execution domain and its routed adapters.
Every direct dependency is declared in [workspace.dependencies] so member crates can never drift onto two versions of the same crate; members only add features.
rusqlite versions must stay aligned across the workspace because libsqlite3-sys carries links="sqlite3", which physically forbids two SQLite bindings in one build.

The release profile is size-tuned (fat LTO, codegen-units=1, opt-level="s", panic=abort, strip), while a separate `lab` profile trades thin LTO and 16 codegen units plus unstripped line-tables symbols for fast rebuilds and perf attribution; shipped artifacts stay on release.

fastwebsockets is pinned exactly to 0.8.1 for its unstable-split feature because a WebSocket read is not cancel-safe and the tunnel needs independent read and write halves; the comment records this supply-chain risk as accepted knowingly.
v8 is pinned to 152.1 because it is the first rusty_v8 release carrying v8::Locker and Send Globals, which celld's shared-isolate design requires.
sqlite-vec is pinned to =0.1.9 to hold the audited C amalgamation exactly because the pre-v1 binding sits outside its compatibility policy.

celld uses tikv-jemallocator with the stats feature because the memory-pressure classifier needs the difference between stats.allocated and stats.resident (allocator-held pages no cell uses) to avoid staying latched on RSS the allocator controls.

1. Adding a policy to the logic core: Add an Event/Effect variant to types.rs, handle it in the match in on_event, and execute it in the actor's effect executor. Validation via cargo + simulation. input.content:
---
type: change-guide
title: "Common Change Guides"
description: "Focused recipes for representative celld maintenance tasks: adding a core policy decision and its executor effect, adding a CELLD_* environment variable, extending the JS API surface, evolving bucket-resident protocol objects, bumping the peer protocol, and touching the storage dialect."
tags: [change-guide, maintenance, testing, env-vars, protocol]
---

Each guide names the owning seam and the narrowest validation that proves the
change. The governing rule everywhere: decisions go to `celld-logic`, effects
go to `celld` adapters, and nothing in between is allowed to drift (see
`openwiki/architecture/logic-decision-core.md` and
`openwiki/architecture/execution-boundary.md`).

## 1. Add a policy decision to the logic core

1. Extend the vocabulary in `crates/logic/types.rs` — a new `Event` variant
   (what the core is told) and/or a new `Effect` variant versioned with
   `op: OpId` (what the core asks for). `Event`/`Effect` are the only I/O of
   the core (`crates/logic/types.rs:3-8, 737-740`).
2. Handle the event inside the `State` method that owns that policy area and
   wire it in the `on_event` dispatcher (`crates/logic/lib.rs:5215+`). If the
   event carries time, give it `now_ms`/`now_mono_ms` stamps so `on_event`'s
   monotonic `max` fold applies (`crates/logic/lib.rs:5215-5223`).
3. Execute the effect in the Actor: add a match arm to
   `Actor::execute` (`crates/celld/actor.rs:2824+`). The established shape is
   to push a future onto `StepOutput` that performs the I/O and returns a
   `CompletedEffect::plain(Event::XxxCompleted { op, .. })` — a stale `op`
   in the completion is then ignored by the core by contract
   (`crates/celld/actor.rs:2829-2845`).
4. If the change touches a lifecycle invariant, extend `State::validate`;
   the executor asserts it after every event whenever `validate_invariants`
   is on (debug builds and simulation; too costly for release traffic)
   (`crates/celld/actor.rs:2794-2796`).

Validation: the conformance world/simulation corpora mount through
`include!(env!(...))` gates (`crates/celld/lib.rs:299-435`), so a policy
change is exercised by the seeded simulation harness; a plain `cargo test`
without the corpus env paths only compiles the gates. See
`openwiki/testing/testing-strategy.md`.

## 2. Add or change a `CELLD_*` environment variable

- Parse it through `crates/celld/env_vars.rs` only: `flag`, `positive`,
  `positive_or`, `parse_optional` (`crates/celld/env_vars.rs:115-180`). The
  contract is *"An unset variable selects its caller's documented default. A
  supplied variable must contain a valid value, so a typo cannot silently
  change the configuration of a running node"* — a Boolean accepts only `0`
  or `1`, and startup exits on invalid values (`crates/celld/env_vars.rs:3-8`,
  `docs/README.md:706-708`).
- If any consumer caches the value or reads it from a synchronous callback
  (so it cannot return an error at the point of use), add the name to
  `env_vars::validate()`'s startup pass, which makes later reads infallible
  without inventing defaults for malformed values
  (`crates/celld/env_vars.rs:10-50`).
- Build policy configuration at the edge, not in the core: e.g. the pressure
  config and ownership-on-evict policy come from `machine.rs` helpers called
  by the Actor (`crates/celld/actor.rs:6-10`), mirroring `logic::pressure`'s
  rule that "the env read that builds the config stays at the edge"
  (`crates/logic/pressure.rs:3-6`).
- Document the variable in the `docs/README.md` environment table.

Validation: the strict parsers are shared, so unit tests of `env_vars` plus
one startup run with the variable set to a bad value (expect exit) cover the
contract.

## 3. Extend the JS API surface (Workers compatibility)

- The per-isolate surface is assembled by `crates/celld/js/bootstrap.rs`:
  fixed prelude/harness scripts are compiled once per process and cached,
  while `env` bindings, the routing table, and compatibility flags differ per
  worker and are built every time (`crates/celld/js/bootstrap.rs:3-8`).
  Ops the JS layer calls back into live in `js.rs` and `js/` child modules
  (`storage_ops.rs`, `r2_ops.rs`, `websocket.rs`, `crypto.rs`, `modules.rs`).
- Remember the domain rule: `js.rs` is the raw V8 arm *outside* the Actor
  execution domain; Actor-reachable wake and WebSocket state is injected
  through `HostServices` rather than reached directly
  (`crates/celld/js.rs:2-5`, `crates/celld/host_services.rs:3-9`).
- If the surface depends on a deployment feature, gate it through the
  manifest feature flags in `crates/celld/protocol.rs` (e.g.
  `FEATURE_KV_V1`, `FEATURE_D1_V1`) (`crates/celld/protocol.rs:54-101`).

Validation: the compatibility promise is checked differentially against
workerd on identical program bytes, and the corpus only grows — a new API
surface needs fixtures that give equal output on both engines
(`docs/testing.md:39-56`). A quick manual loop is `celld dev` with one of
the `examples/` projects (the `counter` example is the standard smoke).

## 4. Change a bucket-resident object layout

`protocol.rs` is the seam: *"Durable types on the bucket contract between
deployment tools and celld. These objects are the interface; nothing else is
exchanged"* (`crates/celld/protocol.rs:1-3`). Objects include the deployment
manifest (`protocol.rs:15`), the `deploy/current.json` fleet pointer
(`protocol.rs:401`, written by `crates/celld/deploy.rs:615-619`, read via
`fleet::CURRENT_POINTER_KEY`, `crates/celld/fleet.rs:628`), the fleet secret
`fleet/peer-auth.json` (`crates/celld/peer_auth.rs:20`), node leases, and
ownership records.

- Layout changes must be safe while old readers and new writers coexist, or
  the release must demand a full stop of every node before switching — the
  docs record exactly which historical upgrades were forced stop-the-world
  and why (`docs/README.md:514-544`).
- A KV-value layout note from v0.4.0: values moved under the ownership epoch
  with an epoch-qualified row reference, and a mixed fleet could make a
  committed value unavailable — the pattern to check against
  (`docs/README.md:535-544`).
- New fleets can share a bucket only through the key prefix
  (`s3://bucket/PREFIX`), so any new key must be built from the same
  prefix-aware path (`README.md:203-208`); `ltx_repl` deliberately builds its
  own clients that carry the prefix because two fleets sharing one bucket
  would otherwise replicate over each other
  (`crates/celld/ltx_repl.rs:3-13`).

Validation: exercise against a real store — `celld diagnose` sends four
conditional writes to the target bucket (`docs/guarantees.md:59-62`) — and
keep restore paths byte-decidable: an LTX takeover reads retained bundles
under the newest safe epoch (`openwiki/concepts/durability-and-replication.md`).

## 5. Bump the peer protocol version

- The single constant is `peer_auth::PROTOCOL_VERSION` (plus its text form),
  carried on ownership/handoff answers and compared on every versioned peer
  request (`crates/celld/actor.rs:2816-2822`,
  `crates/celld/main.rs:1007, 1250`), and negotiated at tunnel establishment
  (`crates/celld/main/peer_tunnel.rs:339`). The tunnel itself is a named h1
  upgrade (`celld-tunnel`) carrying plain HTTP with `x-cells-*` control
  headers (`crates/celld/main/peer_tunnel.rs:3-14, 40`).
- The establishment step is the intended negotiation point: "The tunnel
  establishment carries the version, so a later protocol change can negotiate
  instead of refuse" (`docs/README.md:535-544`). Today refusal is what ships:
  v0.4.0 refuses a different version outright, which is why that upgrade is
  not a rolling update (`docs/README.md:535-544`).
- If the change alters what a stale body could mean, re-check the replay and
  clock-window predicates in `logic/peer.rs` — they are SECURITY fences
  (`crates/logic/peer.rs:3-8`).

Validation: `celld diagnose` reports peers whose protocol versions do not
agree (`docs/README.md:553-568`); the mixed-version handshake is exactly the
`PROTOCOL_VERSION` equality checks above.

## 6. Touch the object-store dialect

`bucket.rs` is the engine's single object-store client, and callers never see
which conditional-write dialect is active: S3/Azure use etag `If-Match` /
`If-None-Match`; GCS uses `x-goog-if-generation-match` because Cloud Storage
does not apply `If-Match` to a PUT (`crates/celld/bucket.rs:3-17`). Preserve
the error contract relied on by self-fencing: `put_cas` answers `Ok(None)`
*only* for a clean 412/409 rejection; everything else is ambiguous (the write
may have committed) and surfaces as `Err`; a response without a CAS token is
an error, never a trusted empty token (`crates/celld/bucket.rs:13-17`).

Validation: run the storage test against the store (`celld diagnose`'s four
conditional writes, `docs/guarantees.md:59-62`) and qualify a store only by
updating the qualified list in `docs/guarantees.md` with the properties it
demonstrates (`docs/guarantees.md:27-44`).

## Change hygiene

- Respect the boundary lints: never call raw `tokio::spawn`/time/`std::fs`
  inside the execution domain; route through `asyncrt`, or place the code in
  a module that documents itself as outside the domain
  (`clippy.toml:1-90`, `crates/celld/Cargo.toml:20-21`).
- Keep the fork of truth small: every direct dependency is versioned once in
  `[workspace.dependencies]` (`Cargo.toml:33-35`).
- Commit messages in this project carry rationale the way the code comments
  do — when a pin, a profile, or a fence looks odd, the explanation belongs
  next to it, not only in the PR.

claims.statement: A new core policy is added by extending the Event/Effect vocabulary in types.rs and dispatching in on_event; time-bearing events must carry now_ms/now_mono_ms stamps so the core clock advances only via the monotonic max fold.

Effects are executed by adding an arm to Actor::execute, which pushes a future onto StepOutput that performs the I/O and replies with a CompletedEffect carrying an Event versioned by the effect's OpId; the core ignores completions whose op is obsolete.

Lifecycle invariant changes are guarded by State::validate, which the executor re-checks after every event when validate_invariants is enabled (debug builds and simulation), because the full cell-table scan is too expensive for release traffic.

CELLD_* variables are parsed only through env_vars helpers with the strict contract: unset selects the documented default, a supplied value must be valid (Booleans accept only 0/1), and celld exits at startup on invalid values rather than defaulting a typo.
Variables whose consumers cache the value or read it synchronously must be added to env_vars::validate's startup pass, making those reads infallible without granting malformed values a default.

Environment-derived policy configuration is built at the edge (machine.rs helpers called by the Actor), never inside celld-logic, mirroring logic::pressure's rule that the env read and the measurement stay outside the pure classifier.

The JS API surface is assembled in js/bootstrap.rs: the prelude and harness compile once per process and are cached, while per-worker bindings (env, routing table, compatibility flags) are built for each isolate.
Every new Workers/DO API surface is validated by differential fixtures run on identical program bytes against workerd and celld, and the conformance corpus only grows.

Bucket-resident objects are the durable contract between deployment tools and celld and are typed in protocol.rs, including the deploy/current.json fleet pointer written by celld deploy and read through fleet::CURRENT_POINTER_KEY.

A bucket key prefix lets two fleets share one bucket, so new keys must be prefix-aware; ltx_repl deliberately builds its own object-store clients that carry the prefix because two fleets replicating over each other is the failure mode.

bucket.rs exposes one object-store client whose CAS token is an opaque read-answered, write-consumed string, hiding the per-provider dialect: S3 and Azure speak etag If-Match/If-None-Match, GCS speaks x-goog-if-generation-match because it ignores If-Match on PUT.

put_cas answers Ok(None) only for a clean 412/409 conditional rejection; every other failure is ambiguous (possibly committed) and surfaces as Err, and a response without a CAS token is an error — this contract is what the self-fence relies on.
The peer protocol version is the single peer_auth::PROTOCOL_VERSION constant, compared on versioned peer requests, attached to handoff adoption answers, and carried on tunnel establishment.

Protocol bumps currently refuse mixed versions (v0.3.0 to v0.4.0 must not be a rolling update because the peer protocol refuses a different version), and the tunnel establishment is documented as the intended negotiation point for future version changes.
Storage-contract changes are validated with the storage test: celld diagnose sends four conditional writes to the target bucket and reports which required property the store fails.
